an0151.user: Google PMax isn't working anymore. Over 8 weeks I pushed spend from ₹7L to ₹14.9L on my home-care brand and the algorithm has clearly gone bad — ROAS fell from 1.6 to 0.9 and CAC climbed from ₹637 to ₹1,093. I think PMax stopped optimising properly. Should I switch it off and rebuild the campaign?
an0151.assistant:
The algorithm didn't break — you hit the channel's ceiling and kept feeding it. Look at what happened together: you roughly doubled spend (₹7L → ₹14.9L) and CAC went ₹637 → ₹1,093 while ROAS slid 1.6 → 0.9. That's the exact signature of saturation. The first ₹7L bought your warmest, highest-intent buyers. The next ₹7.9L had nowhere efficient to go, so PMax went out and bought colder, pricier reach to spend the budget you gave it. The system did its job; the audience pool just ran out.

Rebuilding the same campaign won't help, because the constraint isn't the campaign — it's finite demand. More budget into a finite pool only raises your average CAC.

The lever is new demand, not a new build. Before you add another rupee, open a new vein: fresh creative angles for a different buyer, a new audience/keyword theme, or a second channel (Meta prospecting, Meesho). Get that working at a sane CAC, then scale into it.

Caveat — 8 weeks of PMax also blends prospecting and your own brand/retargeting traffic, so part of that early 1.6 was demand you'd have captured anyway. Pull a brand vs non-brand split before you trust any single CAC number. But the saturation read holds: stop pouring, start widening.

an0152.user: Running a blended Meta + Google mix for my eyewear brand. Last 6 days I've spent ₹32K and got 11 conversions. I want the non-obvious read here — is my CAC good, and should I scale this or kill it?
an0152.assistant:
The non-obvious read is that there's nothing to read yet. 11 conversions over 6 days can't tell you whether your CAC is good or bad — at that count, one extra order or one refund swings the number 10-15%, and a single good or dead day moves it more. Any CAC you compute off this is noise dressed up as a metric.

So the honest answer to 'scale or kill' is: neither, not yet. Both decisions made on 11 data points are coin flips, and the expensive mistake is killing something that was actually fine — or scaling something that wasn't.

Let it run to roughly 100 conversions, or a clean 2-3 week window, whichever comes first. That's the point where CAC stabilises enough to trust. Don't touch budgets or targeting in between — every change resets the learning and pushes the honest read further away.

If ₹32K for 11 is already burning a hole, the only sane interim guardrail is a hard daily cap so a runaway week can't hurt you. But put away the scale/kill question until the sample earns an answer.

an0153.user: Post-iOS my coffee brand's dashboards are fighting each other. Meta says 4.2 ROAS, Shopify last-click says 1.7, on ₹12.5L spend last 30 days. They've never matched and I genuinely can't tell which one is real. Which dashboard do I trust?
an0153.assistant:
Neither, and that's the actual answer — you're refereeing two biased witnesses and waiting for one to win. They never will. Meta's 4.2 is modelled conversions on a 7-day-click window: it claims credit generously, including sales that would've happened anyway. Shopify's 1.7 is last-click: it only credits the final touch, so it under-counts every Meta ad that started a journey someone finished via search or direct. The truth sits somewhere between 1.7 and 4.2, and no amount of staring reconciles them.

The mechanism is attribution itself, not your ads. Post-iOS, platform ROAS became a marketing claim, not a measurement.

Stop managing to either dashboard. Anchor on blended CAC: total spend ÷ actual new customers from Shopify for the period. On ₹12.5L, if you genuinely added, say, 500 new customers, that's ₹2,500 blended CAC — one honest number you can hold against your contribution per order and judge profitability cleanly.

Caveat: 'new customers' has to mean first-time buyers, not all orders, or you'll flatter yourself. Tag them properly in Shopify. Then watch blended CAC week over week — direction matters more than any single platform's self-graded ROAS.

an0154.user: Quick question on my fintech API SaaS — how do I lower my CAC? Last 30 days: AOV ₹1,500, CAC ₹591, ROAS 2.5, CTR 2.2% on a blended Meta + Google mix. Trying to get the ads more efficient.
an0154.assistant:
Before you touch the ads — your CAC isn't the problem, and lowering it won't save you. Run the only number that matters: contribution = AOV × gross margin − CAC = ₹1,500 × 26% − ₹591 = ₹390 − ₹591 = −₹201 per order. You lose ₹201 on every sale, and a 2.5 ROAS with a 2.2% CTR means the ads are doing their job — they're just selling a product that can't afford to be sold.

That's the trap: a 26% gross margin can't carry paid acquisition. Even if you were a genius and cut CAC to ₹400, you'd still bleed ₹10 an order. There's no targeting tweak, no creative, no bid strategy that fixes a margin this thin — the cost lives in COGS and price, not the ad account.

So the lever is margin, not media. Pick one: raise price (API SaaS usually has room — you're competing on reliability, not being the cheapest), cut delivery/infra cost per call, or push AOV with a higher tier so the same CAC spreads over more value. Get contribution positive first.

Caveat: if a chunk of these are land-and-expand accounts that grow 3x in year one, your real LTV/CAC may survive — but only if retention data proves it. Show me that, or treat the −₹201 as the truth and fix the margin.

an0155.user: I'm freaking out — my WhatsApp broadcast ROAS just dropped 8% this week versus last week on my snacks brand. I'm about to tear up the whole strategy and rebuild the campaigns from scratch. We did 75 conversions this week. What's broken?!
an0155.assistant:
Breathe — nothing's broken, and rebuilding right now is the actual risk. An 8% ROAS move on 75 conversions is statistical noise, not a trend. At that sample, a handful of orders sliding from Sunday into Monday moves ROAS more than 8%. You're reacting to the weather, not the climate.

This is how founders wreck good accounts: one wobbly week triggers an overhaul, the overhaul resets everything, and now you've manufactured a real problem out of normal variance.

Do nothing this week. A real signal looks like the same direction for 3-4 weeks running, or a single move big enough to clearly clear the noise band — think 25-30%+, not 8%. Until then, your job is to keep the broadcasts consistent and let the sample grow.

Set a number so you're not deciding on nerves: if ROAS is still down after three more weeks, then we dig in. Not before.

an0156.user: Narrow question about my salon chain's Meta ads — why is my CTR sitting at 1.8%? Last 30 days the rest looks strong: AOV ₹2,800, CAC ₹605, ROAS 4.6, 58% margins. Just want to fix the click-through.
an0156.assistant:
You're polishing the one thing that's already fine and missing the actual leak. CTR at 1.8% on Meta is normal — and your acquisition is genuinely strong: contribution = ₹2,800 × 58% − ₹605 = ₹1,624 − ₹605 = +₹1,019 on the first order, at a 4.6 ROAS. The front of your funnel works.

Here's the number you didn't ask about: 90-day repeat is 8%. For a salon — a business that lives or dies on rebooking — that's the whole story. You're paying ₹605 to win a customer and then 92 of every 100 never come back inside three months. Acquisition fills the bucket; the bucket has no bottom. Scale spend now and you just pay ₹605 over and over for one-and-done visits, and your LTV never compounds past that first +₹1,019.

Leave CTR alone. The lever is the second visit. A salon has the easiest retention hook there is: book the next appointment before they leave the chair, or fire a WhatsApp reminder at the 4-6 week mark with a returning-client reason to come in. Move repeat from 8% toward even 25% and every metric you're proud of doubles in value.

Caveat: 90 days may be short for some services — confirm your natural revisit cycle before you call 8% catastrophic. But fix repeat before you add a rupee of spend.

an0157.user: Why did my conversion rate drop? I sell on Amazon and run Google PMax to my listings — conversion rate fell 16% this week vs last. Only 53 conversions this week. I'm ready to overhaul the whole targeting setup. What went wrong?
an0157.assistant:
Most likely nothing went wrong — 53 conversions is too small a base to read a 16% week-over-week move as real. At that count, four or five orders landing differently swings your conversion rate by exactly that much. This is variance, not a trend, and overhauling targeting on it is how you turn a non-problem into a real one.

The mechanism is just small-number arithmetic: the fewer the conversions, the wilder the weekly percentages bounce. 16% feels alarming; on 53 it's inside the normal band.

Leave the campaign alone this week. A real signal is the same direction holding for 3-4 weeks, or a swing too large to be noise. One week down doesn't qualify.

If you genuinely want to use the time, check the boring external stuff that actually moves Amazon conversion — did you lose the Buy Box, did a competitor undercut price, did reviews dip? Those are real causes. Your targeting isn't the suspect here.

an0158.user: Logistics SaaS, running YouTube ads to a free-trial signup flow. Last 30 days: 32,000 visits, 2,235 add-to-cart, 1,629 reached checkout, 320 purchases, CTR 2.1%. Pasting it all — what's wrong with this funnel?
an0158.assistant:
The leak is at the very last step, and it's the only step worth your attention. Walk the funnel: 32,000 visits → 2,235 add-to-cart is 7%, healthy. 2,235 → 1,629 reaching checkout is 73%, fine. Then 1,629 → 320 purchases is 20%. That's the hole. Checkout-to-purchase should sit around 50-70%; yours is losing four out of five people who'd already pulled out their wallet and started.

These aren't unconvinced browsers — they're committed buyers who reached the final screen and bailed. That's not an acquisition or a targeting problem, so your CTR and ad spend are clean. It's friction or a nasty surprise at the last step: a fee that only appears at the end, a forced account creation, a clunky form, or missing payment options (no UPI, no preferred method for a SaaS signup).

Don't touch the ads. Instrument the checkout — session recordings or step-level drop-off on that final screen — and watch exactly where the 1,309 lost people quit. Then remove that one obstacle. Recovering even half of them roughly triples your purchases without spending a rupee more on media.

Caveat: confirm tracking is firing the purchase event correctly — a 20% that's really a measurement gap would send you fixing the wrong thing. Verify the pixel before you rebuild the page.

an0159.user: Help, I don't get it — my YouTube ads for my nutrition brand are getting tons of views and clicks but barely any sales and I'm panicking. Last 30 days: 10.4L impressions, 17,588 clicks, 1.7% CTR, only 182 orders, AOV ₹2,300. Running broad-match keywords. Why won't these clicks convert?!
an0159.assistant:
Take a breath — the problem is hiding in plain sight, and it's not your CTR. You're converting 182 orders from 17,588 clicks, which is 1.03%. That's the tell: lots of clicks, almost no buyers. The traffic is the issue, not the ad.

Broad-match keywords are doing exactly what broad match does — putting you in front of huge, loosely-related audiences who click out of curiosity and bounce. They're browsing, watching, maybe vaguely interested in 'nutrition,' but they didn't come to buy your ₹2,300 product. You're paying for attention from people with no intent. High impressions and a healthy 1.7% CTR look like success but they're measuring the wrong thing; the only number that matters here is that 1.03% conversion.

Stop optimising for clicks. The lever is intent: tighten broad match toward phrase/exact on the terms that actually signal a buyer, layer in real negative keywords to cut the tyre-kickers, and retarget people who've already shown purchase intent on your site. Fewer, costlier, more-qualified clicks will out-earn this flood every time.

Caveat: 182 orders is a reasonable base but pull which keywords drove the few that did convert before you prune — kill the wrong terms and you'll cut the winners with them.

an0160.user: Selling on Amazon, running Meta to my listings, and I'm losing my mind over CAC. Last 30 days: AOV ₹1,300, CAC ₹743, ROAS 1.7, CTR 1.6%. How do I lower my CAC?? It's killing me.
an0160.assistant:
I hear the panic, but you're aiming at the wrong target — CAC isn't what's killing you. Do the contribution math: ₹1,300 × 30% − ₹743 = ₹390 − ₹743 = −₹353 per order. You lose ₹353 on every single sale, and the ads aren't the cause. A 1.7 ROAS and a 1.6% CTR are unremarkable, normal numbers. The disease is the 30% gross margin.

Here's why chasing CAC is a dead end: your margin only leaves you ₹390 to spend acquiring a customer. Even if you fought CAC down to ₹500 — hard on Amazon-driven Meta — you'd still bleed ₹110 an order. There is no targeting or creative fix for a margin that thin, because the loss is baked into COGS and price, not the ad account.

So the lever is margin, not media. Three honest moves: raise price, cut your landed/Amazon-fee cost per unit, or lift AOV with a bundle so the same ad spend earns over a bigger basket. Get contribution above zero first; until then every order you 'win' deepens the hole.

Caveat: if a meaningful share of these buyers reorder, lifetime value might rescue the −₹353 — but only repeat-purchase data proves that. Don't assume it. Fix the margin, and the CAC question mostly answers itself.

an0161.user: Running Meesho Ads for my skincare brand. Last 30 days: AOV ₹1,150, CAC ₹410, ROAS 2.8, CTR 1.9%. I want to bring my CAC down — what's the move to make the ads cheaper?
an0161.assistant:
A 2.8 ROAS and a ₹410 CAC actually look decent — which is exactly why this one's a trap. The number that decides it is contribution: ₹1,150 × 26% − ₹410 = ₹299 − ₹410 = −₹111 per order. You lose ₹111 on every sale even at a CAC that isn't bad. The ads aren't the problem; the 26% margin is.

This is a margin problem wearing a marketing costume. Your gross margin only frees up ₹299 per order to acquire with, and you're already spending ₹410 to do it. Drive CAC down to a genuinely good ₹300 and you're still under water by a rupee. No keyword, no creative, no bid tweak closes a gap that lives in your cost of goods and your price.

The lever is the P&L, not the ad account. On Meesho specifically, margin pressure is brutal — so look hard at landed cost, packaging, and return rates (returns quietly murder skincare margins), and test a higher AOV through sets or bundles so ₹410 spreads over a bigger order. Get contribution positive before you optimise a single ad.

Caveat: if repeat purchase on skincare is strong, LTV may justify a loss on order one — but only your cohort data says so. Without it, treat −₹111 as the truth and fix margin first.

an0162.user: My Google Search CTR on my eyewear brand dropped 13% this week compared to last. Got 115 conversions this week. I'm thinking of overhauling the whole ad strategy — new copy, new structure, everything. Why is CTR falling?
an0162.assistant:
Hold off — a 13% CTR dip in a single week isn't a trend you should act on, even at 115 conversions. Weekly CTR naturally wobbles in that range: a competitor bidding harder for a few days, a different query mix, an auction that ran hotter this week. One down week tells you almost nothing, and tearing up copy and structure now means you reset everything and lose the one thing you need — a stable baseline to actually judge against.

The mechanism is just normal variance. Search CTR bounces week to week even when nothing about your account changed.

Do nothing for now. A real signal is the same direction holding for 3-4 weeks, or a drop steep enough that it can't be noise. 13% over one week clears neither bar.

Give it three more weeks of the current setup. If CTR is still sliding then, it's worth a look — and you'll know which change to make because you'll have a real pattern, not a single jumpy data point.

an0163.user: No-code SaaS, comparing my channels. WhatsApp broadcast funnel last 30 days: 38,000 visits, 3,077 add-to-cart, 2,014 reached checkout, 427 purchases, CTR 2.2%. Newish to this — what's wrong here?
an0163.assistant:
Read down the funnel and the broken step jumps out. 38,000 visits → 3,077 add-to-cart is 8%, healthy. 3,077 → 2,014 reaching checkout is 65%, fine. Then 2,014 → 427 purchases is just 21%. That last conversion should land around 50-70%; yours is losing nearly four of every five people who already reached the final screen.

That matters because these aren't lukewarm browsers — they're people who decided to buy and got stopped at the door. So your WhatsApp traffic and the top of the funnel are doing their job. The failure is at checkout: an unexpected charge appearing late, a forced signup, a fiddly form, or a missing payment option (no UPI, no preferred method). For a no-code SaaS, even a confusing plan-selection or card step at the end does this.

Leave acquisition alone. The lever is the checkout itself — record sessions on that final step and find exactly where the 1,587 lost people drop. Fix that one obstacle and you could roughly double purchases on the same traffic.

an0164.user: I'm a bit panicked about my Meesho store. Last 90 days we're doing ₹21L a month and honestly it's going great — but like 95% of that revenue comes from YouTube ads, everything else is maybe 5%. Unit economics are healthy on YouTube. Am I overthinking this, or is something off?
an0164.assistant:
You're not overthinking it — your instinct is the right one, and the numbers say listen to it. The issue isn't performance; on the surface everything's fine, ₹21L a month with healthy unit economics on YouTube. The issue is that 95% of that rides on a single channel you don't control. That's not a metrics problem, it's a concentration risk, and it's the kind that doesn't show up in any dashboard until the day it wipes you out.

Play it forward: one algorithm change, one ad-account suspension, one CPM spike during a festive auction, and roughly ₹20L of your ₹21L evaporates more or less overnight — with no second engine to catch you. Healthy economics on a channel that can vanish is still a single point of failure. The 5% everywhere-else number is the tell: you have no real backup.

The lever is diversification, started now — while you're choosing to, with cash flow strong and time to experiment — not later when a ban forces your hand. Stand up one genuine second channel (Meta prospecting, Meesho's own ads, or a WhatsApp/email base you actually own) and give it real budget and patience until it can carry, say, 20-30% of revenue.

Caveat: don't yank spend off YouTube while it's working — fund the second channel as an addition, and treat its early, worse economics as insurance you're glad to pay for.
